title: Reading Brain and Retina from the Surface
endLine: Surface electrodes sum many cells, revealing timing and state, not cause.

scenes.tts: How can you read a working brain without opening it? Rest electrodes on the surface, and listen to many cells at once. They record summed electrical activity from the brain or the retina without entering a cell.
scenes.caption: How can you read a working brain without opening it? Rest electrodes on the surface, and listen to many cells at once. They record summed electrical activity from the brain or the retina without entering a cell.
scenes.visual: Carried world opens full-frame: on the left, a large schematic cross-section of an intact head, brain, and eye (filling 65% of frame height); surface electrodes settle gently onto the scalp before narration names them. Inside the cortex, many tiny glowing cellular currents pulse and sum into one continuous scrolling voltage wave on the right, labelled 'Schematic'.
scenes.narration: How can you read a working brain without opening it? Rest electrodes on the surface, and listen to many cells at once. They record summed electrical activity from the brain or the retina without entering a cell.

scenes.visual: The carried head and slowly scrolling schematic voltage wave dim softly behind the clean, high-contrast title 'Reading Brain and Retina from the Surface', then brighten back into full contrast.

scenes.tts: An electroencephalogram, or E E G, mostly reflects summed synaptic and dendritic currents, picked up at the scalp. To score sleep stages, polysomnography adds two more surface traces. An electro-oculogram tracks eye movements, and a chin electromyogram tracks muscle tone. The night is cut into thirty-second epochs, and each slice gets one stage.
scenes.caption: An electroencephalogram, or EEG, mostly reflects summed synaptic and dendritic currents, picked up at the scalp. To score sleep stages, polysomnography adds two more surface traces. An electro-oculogram tracks eye movements, and a chin electromyogram tracks muscle tone. The night is cut into 30-second epochs, and each slice gets one stage.
scenes.visual: On the carried head, tiny glowing currents along cortical dendrites sum into the top scrolling trace labelled 'EEG (schematic)'. Two additional surface electrodes land beside the eye and on the chin before being named, splitting the right panel into three synced scrolling traces ('EEG', 'Eye movement', 'Chin muscle', all schematic). A vertical '30 s epoch' window sweeps across the traces, stamping each slice with a stage label.
scenes.narration: An electroencephalogram, or EEG, mostly reflects summed synaptic and dendritic currents, picked up at the scalp. To score sleep stages, polysomnography adds two more surface traces. An electro-oculogram tracks eye movements, and a chin electromyogram tracks muscle tone. The night is cut into 30-second epochs, and each slice gets one stage.

scenes.tts: Every surface trace sums many active cells, revealing timing and state rather than single spikes. Flash a pattern, and scalp electrodes over visual cortex catch a visual evoked potential, a wave locked to the stimulus. Move the electrodes to the eye, and the electroretinogram, or E R G, sums the retina's voltage during a flash.
scenes.caption: Every surface trace sums many active cells, revealing timing and state rather than single spikes. Move the electrodes to the eye, and the electroretinogram, or ERG, sums the retina's voltage during a flash.
scenes.visual: The eye and chin electrodes fade back, keeping the carried head and single scrolling trace. A light stimulus pulses into the eye and lights up visual cortex, driving a sharp timed deflection labelled 'Evoked potential (schematic)' on the trace. Camera smoothly zooms into the eye at the front of the same head, transforming the left view into a retina between two surface electrodes as a flash drives a scrolling 'ERG (schematic)' wave on the right.
scenes.narration: Every surface trace sums many active cells, revealing timing and state rather than single spikes. scenes.tts: Inside the retina, photoreceptors drive bipolar cells, which then drive ganglion cells. Photoreceptors and most bipolar cells use graded potentials, smooth voltage shifts, while ganglion cells fire spikes. A transretinal E R G, across a retina removed from the eye, sums all those layers. To read only the photoreceptors, what must you block first?
scenes.caption: Inside the retina, photoreceptors drive bipolar cells, which then drive ganglion cells. Photoreceptors and most bipolar cells use graded potentials, smooth voltage shifts, while ganglion cells fire spikes. A transretinal ERG, across a retina removed from the eye, sums all those layers. To read only the photoreceptors, what must you block first?
scenes.visual: The carried retina cross-section expands to show three linked cell layers left-to-right: photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and ganglion cells (schematic, no molecular structures). Smooth glowing voltage waves swell through photoreceptors and bipolar cells before triggering brief spike ticks at ganglion cells; currents from all three layers merge into one summed transretinal ERG trace on the right. A question mark hovers over the summed trace (do not highlight the synapses yet: that is the answer).
scenes.narration: Inside the retina, photoreceptors drive bipolar cells, which then drive ganglion cells. Photoreceptors and most bipolar cells use graded potentials, smooth voltage shifts, while ganglion cells fire spikes. A transretinal ERG, across a retina removed from the eye, sums all those layers. scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause on the same carried retina and summed trace: the question 'What must you block to read only photoreceptors?' sits boldly at the top while downstream synaptic junctions pulse gently and a slow 4.5-second progress bar glides across the bottom.

scenes.tts: You block downstream synaptic responses. Bipolar and ganglion cells get light signals only through those synapses. So once they fall silent, the voltage across the retina reports the photoreceptors.
scenes.caption: You block downstream synaptic responses. Bipolar and ganglion cells get light signals only through those synapses. So once they fall silent, the voltage across the retina reports the photoreceptors.
scenes.visual: Clean block bars clamp onto the synapses downstream of the photoreceptors, dimming bipolar and ganglion activity so the scrolling ERG trace on the right reshapes smoothly into a clean 'Photoreceptors only (schematic)' wave.
scenes.narration: You block downstream synaptic responses. Bipolar and ganglion cells get light signals only through those synapses. So once they fall silent, the voltage across the retina reports the photoreceptors.

scenes.tts: The numbers also depend on the method. Looking tests watch where a baby gazes, to find the finest stripes it can see. At the same age, scalp visual evoked potentials report sharper vision than looking tests do.
scenes.caption: The numbers also depend on the method. Looking tests watch where a baby gazes, to find the finest stripes it can see. At the same age, scalp visual evoked potentials report sharper vision than looking tests do.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls smoothly back out from the eye to the carried head with scalp electrodes over visual cortex. A baby's gaze turns toward a striped patch beside a plain one. Beside the scrolling trace, two high-contrast comparison bars grow with no numbers: 'Looking test' and a taller bar 'Scalp VEP: sharper at same age' (schematic).
scenes.narration: The numbers also depend on the method. Looking tests watch where a baby gazes, to find the finest stripes it can see. At the same age, scalp visual evoked potentials report sharper vision than looking tests do.

scenes.tts: A recording shows activity goes with a stimulus or choice, not that the brain uses it. Take sleep pressure, Process S, which builds while awake and drains in sleep. Deep-sleep slow waves at night's start are larger after longer waking. Yet those E E G waves are a marker of S, not S itself.

scenes.visual: Comparison bars clear; on the carried head, a stimulus flashes alongside cortical waves on the trace, joined by a dashed label 'Goes with ≠ used by brain'. The head then shifts into deep sleep: a gauge labelled 'Process S (schematic)' rises during waking and drains in sleep; large slow EEG waves at the start of the night are bigger after a longer waking bar, linked to the gauge by a dashed tag 'Marker, not S itself'.

scenes.tts: Within those limits, they unlocked findings. In 2015, Vinberg and colleagues used that blocked E R G on mouse retinas at thirty-seven degrees Celsius. In light adaptation, rods turn down their sensitivity, partly through calcium. Rods lacked the two G cap proteins, recoverin, or all three calcium sensors. Calcium-dependent adaptation still persisted without them.
scenes.caption: Within those limits, they unlocked findings. In 2015, Vinberg and colleagues used that blocked ERG on mouse retinas at 37 degrees Celsius. In light adaptation, rods turn down their sensitivity, partly through calcium. Rods lacked the two GCAP proteins, recoverin, or all three calcium sensors. Calcium-dependent adaptation still persisted without them.
scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly back into the carried isolated retina between transretinal electrodes with downstream synapses blocked, tagged '37 °C' and 'Vinberg and colleagues, 2015'. A steady background light comes on and the rod response shrinks (light adaptation, schematic). On the right, two schematic traces overlay: 'normal rods' and 'rods lacking all three sensors' (GCAPs + recoverin), and adaptation still appears in the second ('Schematic', no molecular structures).
scenes.narration: Within those limits, they unlocked findings. In 2015, Vinberg and colleagues used that blocked ERG on mouse retinas at 37 degrees Celsius. scenes.tts: In 2019, Fultz and colleagues tracked slow E E G rhythms in thirteen sleeping people. Slow rhythms were followed by pulses of flow in cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid bathing the brain. That is a correlation, and mouse tracer studies disagree whether waste clearance rises or falls during sleep. Surface waves map the crowd's timing and state, leaving cause for other tests.

scenes.visual: Camera pulls back to the carried sleeping head with scalp electrodes, tagged '13 people — Fultz and colleagues, 2019'. On the right, large slow EEG waves roll across the trace, each wave followed by a glowing pulse of fluid sweeping around the brain labelled 'Cerebrospinal fluid flow (schematic)'. A crisp hedge tag 'Correlation — clearance debated' appears as the carried traces settle into a calm scrolling rhythm.
